title: He skipped off the gunrest and looked gravely at his watcher, gathering about his legs the loose folds of his gown
html_source:
The generally heroic description of Buck Mulligan and the general anti-heroic description of Stephen is part of the gender mesh of Ulysses.

“In designing Ulysses Joyce first identified what the socially conditioned reader is most likely to want and expect from male and female characters of different ages, and then he provides his readers with characters of different ages, and then provides his readers with characters who frustrate and implicitly challenge that desire (Vicki Mahaffey, ”Ulysses and the End of Gender", in Margot Norris (ed.), A Companion to James Joyce’s “Ulysses” (p. 153).

PROPOSED SUGGESTION: Gender and Ulysses is fascinating, but how does this particular moment relate to questions of gender? The flowing gown? The “watcher”? “Heroic” as a traditionally masculine trait? And … “not being heroic” feminine? To be honest, without having read Mahaffey’s essay through, I’m sceptical of the assertion that Joyce began his characters programatically to invert or disrupt cultural expectations of gender. There are plenty of ways to approach gender in Ulysses, and this seems way oversimplified. But again, I haven’t read the essay in question, and I’m sure it has a broader vision than that.

What do you actually mean by “heroic” and “non-heroic”, and what exactly is it about either characters' presentations that invites these adjectives? Do you mean Mulligan has a “mock-heroic” air? Are you making a reference to the Odyssey as it underpins Ulysses? Do you simply mean “heroic” as “like a hero”? The word “heroic” is far too complicated to just leave hanging like this, imo.
